unit.title: Tyres and pit stops
unit.summary: Compounds, degradation, the stop, and the first idea of strategy.

lessons.title: Why tyres decide races
lessons.objective: Explain that tyres are the main performance variable in a race.

payload.prompt: Why do tyres matter more than driver skill in a race?

options.text: Tyre grip fades over a stint, so managing it wins races; all drivers are fast enough.
options.explanation: Right. All drivers in F1 are quick, so the car and tyre strategy decide it.

options.text: The driver's skill is the only thing that matters; tyres are secondary.
options.explanation: Wrong. In modern F1, tyre management is the core of winning.

options.text: Tyres always last the whole race if they are the right compound.
options.explanation: No. Even the right compound wears and degrades lap by lap.

options.text: The team only needs to pick the softest tyre and the driver will win.
options.explanation: Softest is fastest early but dies first. Balancing life and pace is the game.

explanation.correct: Right. Tyre degradation is the main variable. All drivers are quick; the one who manages tyres best finishes ahead.
explanation.incorrect: Tyres degrade over a stint: faster early, slower late. Managing that decay is what separates the winners from the rest.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tyre management is the whole race.

payload.prompt: A driver has old tyres and is ten seconds behind. What is the issue?

options.text: The old tyres have lost grip, so lap times have dropped; a stop is needed soon.
options.explanation: Right. Old tyres degrade past their useful life. Pitting for fresh rubber is the answer.

options.text: The driver is just slow today and needs to push harder.
options.explanation: No. If tyres are old, pushing only ruins them faster. The stop is urgent.

options.text: Old tyres are actually more stable and should be kept until the end.
options.explanation: Wrong. Old tyres have lost grip completely. They are dangerous to keep.

options.text: The problem is the circuit, not the tyres.
options.explanation: Tyre degradation is a universal fact. The circuit may make it faster or slower, but it happens on every track.

explanation.correct: Right. Tyre degradation costs lap time. When a driver is suddenly slow, old tyres are the first suspect.
explanation.incorrect: Tyre degradation is inevitable. The tyres lose grip lap by lap, and when they reach a cliff, the driver loses seconds per lap.
explanation.sayThisLine: The degradation got him; time to pit.

payload.prompt: What does 'tyre management' mean in a race?

options.text: Driving smoothly to keep tyres cool and extend their life, sometimes at the cost of speed.
options.explanation: Right. Managing tyres means pacing yourself early to make them last longer into the stint.

options.text: Pushing flat out from the start so the tyres wear out faster.
options.explanation: That is the opposite. Smooth driving saves tyres; pushing kills them.

options.text: Only the pit crew can manage tyres by picking the right compound.
options.explanation: The crew picks the compound, but the driver's smoothness on track is tyre management.

options.text: Tyres cannot be managed; they wear at a fixed rate no matter what the driver does.
options.explanation: Wrong. How the driver treats the tyres (smooth or aggressive) changes how fast they wear.

explanation.correct: Right. Tyre management is the driver's job: smooth inputs, patience on corner exit, and saving tyres for a late-race push.
explanation.incorrect: Managing tyres means driving smoothly early in the stint to make them last. It costs a bit of speed early but buys you pace late.
explanation.sayThisLine: Good tyre management got him to the end.

payload.prompt: A driver starts on soft tyres on a hot track. How many laps until the tyres hit their performance cliff?

explanation.summary: Soft tyres on a hot track wear fast. A typical cliff for softs is 15 to 20 laps before grip drops sharply.
explanation.sayThisLine: The softs are gone after twenty laps.

payload.prompt: On the same hot track, how long do hard tyres last before hitting the cliff?

explanation.summary: Hard tyres are built for distance. On a hot track, they may last 35 to 40 laps before the cliff, but they are slower early.
explanation.sayThisLine: The hards lasted almost the whole race.

lessons.title: Hard, Medium, Soft
lessons.objective: Read the sidewall colours and the trade-off between grip and life.

payload.prompt: What does a red sidewall on a Pirelli tyre mean?

image.alt: A Pirelli Formula 1 tyre with a red sidewall marking.

options.text: Soft compound: fastest grip, dies quickly.
Hard compound: slowest but lasts the longest.
Intermediate tyre for damp conditions.
Medium compound: a balance of pace and life.

cues: Soft tyres are chosen for qualifying and early stints.

explanation.correct: Right. Red sidewall is the soft compound. It has the most grip but wears fastest.
explanation.incorrect: Red sidewall means soft. Softs are the fastest tyre but the life is short, so they die fast.
explanation.sayThisLine: The reds are the soft compound.

payload.prompt: What does a white sidewall mean?

image.alt: A Pirelli Formula 1 tyre with a white sidewall marking.

options.text: Hard compound: slowest but longest life.
Soft compound: fastest and lightest.
Medium compound: the middle choice.
Intermediate for light rain.

cues: Hards are for long stints and one-stop strategies.

explanation.correct: Right. White sidewall is the hard compound. It lasts longest but grip is lower.
explanation.incorrect: White sidewall is hard. Hards are slow but they last a long time, so they suit distance over speed.
explanation.sayThisLine: Whites are the hard tyre.

payload.prompt: What does a yellow sidewall mean?

image.alt: A Pirelli Formula 1 tyre with a yellow sidewall marking.

options.text: Medium compound: balance of pace and life.
Soft compound: quick but does not last.
Hard compound: built for distance.
Intermediate tyre for wet conditions.

cues: Mediums are often used for the second stint.

explanation.correct: Right. Yellow sidewall is the medium compound. It sits between soft and hard.
explanation.incorrect: Yellow sidewall is medium. Mediums are a jack-of-all-trades tyre: quicker than hard, last longer than soft.
explanation.sayThisLine: The yellows are the medium.

payload.prompt: Match each tyre to its characteristic.

pairs.definition: Maximum grip, fastest per lap, wears out quickly. Used in qualifying and early race stints.
A middle ground between grip and life; often used in the second stint or as a bridge tyre.
Lowest grip of the three, but lasts longest. Built for long stints and one-stop strategies.

distractorDefinitions: The tyre used only in wet weather.
A tyre that cannot be used in the dry.

explanation.summary: The three dry compounds are soft (red, fast), medium (yellow, balanced) and hard (white, durable). Softer = quicker but shorter life.
explanation.sayThisLine: Softs are red, mediums are yellow, hards are white.

payload.prompt: Why would a team choose soft tyres for a pit stop if they have only 15 laps to go?

options.text: Softs give maximum grip for those final laps, even if they only last to the end.
options.explanation: Right. If the stint is short, speed matters more than life. Softs are the fastest tyre.

options.text: Softs are cheaper than hard or medium tyres.
options.explanation: Tyre cost is not the issue; performance is. Softs are picked for pace.

options.text: Softs last longer than mediums in the final laps.
options.explanation: Wrong. Softs wear faster than mediums. But if the stint is short, pace beats durability.

options.text: Hard tyres are never used in the final stint.
options.explanation: Hards are often used at the end of the race if the stint is long enough.

explanation.correct: Right. With only 15 laps left, tyre life does not matter. Softs are the fastest and that is what wins the race.
explanation.incorrect: Soft tyres are the fastest, even if they die soon. In a short final stint, pace matters more than durability.
explanation.sayThisLine: They went soft for the final sprint.

payload.prompt: A team chooses hard tyres for the first stint at the start. What is the strategy?

options.text: Build a long first stint to control the race, then stop late for softs for a late push.
options.explanation: Right. Hards are durable, so starting on them lets the team run long and pit late.

options.text: Hards are always faster than softs, so they start the race.
options.explanation: Wrong. Softs are faster. Hards are chosen for durability, not speed.

options.text: Hard tyres are mandatory for the race start.
options.explanation: No. Any of the three compounds can start the race.

options.text: The driver prefers hard tyres for comfort.
options.explanation: Comfort is not the reason. Strategy and track conditions dictate the choice.

explanation.correct: Right. Starting on hards is a patience strategy: run long, pit late, and finish on fresher tyres than rivals.
explanation.incorrect: Hard-first is about strategy: hards last longer, so you stay out longer and pit late for a quicker tyre.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hard first, then a late stop for softs.

lessons.title: Intermediates and full wets
lessons.objective: Choose the right wet tyre for a given track condition.

payload.prompt: It is raining but the track is drying. Should you use inters or full wets?

facts.label: Rainfall
facts.value: Light to moderate rain, not torrential.

facts.label: Standing water
facts.value: Some puddles in two corners, most of the track is damp.

options.label: Intermediates
options.consequence: The inters work on a damp, drying track. They have enough water dispersal and will be faster than wets as the track clears.
considerations: Light to moderate rain suits inters.
The track is drying, so inters will be quicker soon.

options.label: Full wets
options.consequence: Full wets are safe in the wet, but they are slower than inters on a drying track. You may need to pit for inters in a few laps.
considerations: Wets are safer in heavy rain, but here the rain is light and drying.

payload.expertNote: Inters are for damp and drying; wets are for heavy rain and standing water. The crossover point is key: when the track is faster on slicks than inters, pit for inters or slicks.
payload.sayThisLine: Inters on the drying track, they will work better than wets.

payload.prompt: It is pouring rain with standing water in several corners. Inters or wets?

facts.label: Standing water
facts.value: Deep puddles on several sections; visibility is poor.

facts.label: Forecast
facts.value: Rain continues for the rest of the race.

options.label: Full wets
options.consequence: Full wets are designed for this. The grooves disperse heavy water and prevent aquaplaning. Inters would lose time and risk crashes.
considerations: Heavy rain and standing water demand full wets.
Safety first: inters cannot handle this volume of water.

options.label: Intermediates
options.consequence: Inters will lose grip on the standing water and risk aquaplaning or crashes. Not safe.
considerations: Inters are for damp, not torrents.

payload.expertNote: Full wets are the only choice in heavy rain. They have deeper grooves and a softer compound to grip in the wet.
payload.sayThisLine: Full wets in the heavy rain, no question.

payload.prompt: The track is drying fast and you are now faster on inters than on wets. Should you pit for inters?

scene.alt: A track drying lap by lap, with a car on full wets getting slower each time.

explanation.correct: Right. When the crossover point hits and inters are faster, you pit immediately. Staying on wets costs time.
explanation.incorrect: The crossover point is when the dry tyre becomes faster than the wet tyre. Pit for it immediately.

payload.prompt: In qualifying, a light rain is falling. Is an intermediate tyre good for a qualifying lap?

scene.alt: A car on the track in light rain, with a partly wet and partly drying surface.

explanation.correct: Right. Light rain is perfect for inters. They have good water dispersal and are faster than wets in drying conditions.
explanation.incorrect: Intermediates are ideal for damp and light-rain qualifying. They are faster than wets and safer than slicks on a wet track.

payload.prompt: Why are inters faster than full wets on a damp track?

options.text: Inters have less deep grooves, so less drag and more contact patch on damp surfaces.
options.explanation: Right. Inters give more grip and less water resistance on damp conditions. Wets are designed for torrents.

options.text: Full wets are always slower no matter the conditions.
options.explanation: Wrong. Full wets are faster in heavy rain. They are just too thick for damp conditions.

options.text: Inters have more grip because they are made of softer rubber.
options.explanation: Both are soft rubber. The difference is groove depth and compound. Inters have shallower grooves for damp.

options.text: Full wets cannot handle any water and are only for dry days.
options.explanation: Wrong. Full wets are for heavy water. Inters are for damp.

explanation.correct: Right. Inters are optimised for damp: less groove depth means more grip and less drag on damp surfaces.
explanation.incorrect: Inters are designed for damp and drying tracks. Wets are for heavy rain and standing water.
explanation.sayThisLine: Inters are better on the drying track.

lessons.title: Degradation, graining, blistering and the cliff
lessons.objective: Name the four ways a tyre loses grip and what each looks like.

payload.prompt: Match each tyre death mode to its description.

pairs.definition: The gradual loss of grip over a stint as the compound wears away.
Tiny rubber balls tear off and roughen the surface, costing grip temporarily but potentially reversible.
Overheating causes bubbles to form and permanently damage the tyre.
The sudden collapse in grip when a tyre reaches the end of its useful life, dropping five seconds per lap.

distractorDefinitions: A tyre that has a slow puncture and loses air gradually.
A flat-spotted tyre from hard braking on a cold track.

explanation.summary: Tyres die in four ways: degradation (slow wear), graining (temporary roughness), blistering (heat damage) and the cliff (sudden collapse).
explanation.sayThisLine: His tyres have hit the cliff.

payload.prompt: Match each tyre problem to what causes it.

pairs.definition: Happens when the track is cool and the tyre cannot heat up enough, so rubber balls tear off.
Too much heat from long stints or hard braking; the rubber overheats and bubbles form.
Normal wear from lap after lap; the tyre compound is slowly abraded away.

distractorDefinitions: The driver changing gear too quickly.

explanation.summary: Graining = cold track, blistering = hot track, degradation = normal wear over distance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Blistering from the heat.

payload.prompt: A driver is on old soft tyres and suddenly loses five seconds per lap. What happened?

options.text: The tyres hit the cliff: grip collapsed suddenly, not gradually.
options.explanation: Right. The tyre cliff is sudden and catastrophic, not slow wear.

options.text: The track got slower as the sun set.
options.explanation: The cliff is about the tyre, not the track. The tyre lost grip suddenly.

options.text: The driver made a mistake and lost concentration.
options.explanation: No. A five-second drop across the board is the tyre, not the driver.

options.text: The pit wall told the driver to go slower.
options.explanation: A sudden five-second drop is the tyre cliff, not a call from the pit wall.

explanation.correct: Right. The tyre cliff is the sudden end of grip. It is not gradual; the tyre goes from usable to dead in one lap.
explanation.incorrect: The tyre cliff is a sudden collapse in grip when the compound reaches the end of its life. It costs five seconds or more immediately.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cliff hit him and he lost the place.

payload.prompt: A driver has graining on the front tyres. Can it be fixed?

options.text: Maybe. Warming the tyre up can help the graining go away temporarily, but it may come back.
options.explanation: Right. Graining can reverse if the tyre heats up enough. Blistering is permanent damage.

options.text: No, graining is permanent like blistering.
options.explanation: Wrong. Graining can recover if the tyre warms. Blistering is forever.

options.text: Graining just means the tyre needs more pressure.
options.explanation: Pressure helps, but graining is about rubber temperature and surface texture.

options.text: It is not graining; the driver is just going slower.
options.explanation: Graining is a real tyre problem. It costs grip and pace.

explanation.correct: Right. Graining is temporary and can reverse with heat. Blistering is permanent and the tyre must be changed.
explanation.incorrect: Graining happens when the tyre is too cold. Warm it up and the grip may come back. Blistering is permanent heat damage.
explanation.sayThisLine: The graining went away once the tyre warmed up.

payload.prompt: On a very hot track, at what tyre operating temperature does blistering begin to risk?

explanation.summary: Soft tyres can safely run up to about 110 to 115 degrees Celsius. Beyond that, blistering risk rises sharply.
explanation.sayThisLine: The tyres are at 115 degrees and blistering is starting.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a pit stop
lessons.objective: Order the steps of a stop and explain what makes it fast or slow.

payload.prompt: Put the steps of a pit stop in order.

items.text: The driver enters the pit box and stops on the marks.
items.why: The car must be in the right position for the crew to work.

items.text: The jacks lift the car and the wheels are loosened and removed.
items.why: The old tyres come off quickly; four mechanics work in parallel.

items.text: Fresh tyres are fitted and tightened, fuel is added if needed.
items.why: New tyres go on and are torqued; fuel flows if the race is long.

items.text: The jacks are lowered and the driver is released back onto the track.
items.why: The stop is complete; the driver re-enters the race.

explanation.correct: Right. That is a pit stop: stop, lift, change tyres, lower, go.
explanation.incorrect: A pit stop is: car stops on marks, jacks up the car, old wheels off and new wheels on, jacks down, driver released.

payload.prompt: A top team performs a pit stop in 2 seconds of stationary time. What is happening?

scene.alt: Overhead view of a pit box: jacks up, four wheels coming off and four going on simultaneously.

explanation.summary: A two-second stop has all four wheels removed and fitted in parallel, so only one rotation time per wheel.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two seconds, that is a perfect stop.

payload.prompt: On a typical circuit, how much time does a driver lose by pitting compared to staying on track?

explanation.summary: Pit loss is about 20 to 25 seconds at most circuits: time through the pit lane (slowed), the stop itself (two seconds), and exiting.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pit loss is about twenty seconds.

payload.prompt: What makes a pit stop faster: car position, crew skill, or tyre preparation?

options.text: All three: the car must be in the right spot, the crew must be co-ordinated, and the new tyres must be ready.
options.explanation: Right. A fast stop needs perfect execution across all three.

options.text: Only crew skill matters; the car position does not matter.
options.explanation: Car position matters hugely. If the car is not centred, the crew cannot work.

options.text: Only tyre preparation matters; the crew is secondary.
options.explanation: Tyre prep helps, but crew co-ordination is what delivers the two-second stop.

options.text: The crew speed does not matter if the tyres are prepared in advance.
options.explanation: Crew speed is essential. Even with ready tyres, bad execution loses time.

explanation.correct: Right. A fast pit stop is a perfect routine: precise car placement, trained crew working in unison, and new tyres at hand.
explanation.incorrect: Fast pit stops require all three: good car positioning in the box, a co-ordinated crew, and new tyres ready to fit.
explanation.sayThisLine: A perfect stop: the car was in and the crew was ready.

payload.prompt: What is an unsafe release?

options.text: Releasing the car from the pit box when a wheel is not secure, or into the path of another car.
options.explanation: Right. Unsafe release is a pit-lane infraction that earns a penalty.

options.text: Releasing the car too early in the race.
options.explanation: That does not make sense. Release is done at the end of a stop.

options.text: When the pit crew does not signal the driver clearly.
options.explanation: Poor communication is not an unsafe release; it is a crew mistake.

options.text: Releasing the car on a wet day.
options.explanation: Weather does not define an unsafe release. The issue is unsecured wheels or traffic.

explanation.correct: Right. An unsafe release is a pit infraction: loose wheel or into another car's path. Usually earns a time penalty.
explanation.incorrect: An unsafe release is when the car leaves the pit box with a loose wheel or into the path of oncoming traffic. It is a penalty.
explanation.sayThisLine: That was an unsafe release from the pits.

lessons.title: The two-compound rule
lessons.objective: Explain why every dry race has at least one stop.

payload.prompt: Why does F1 have a two-compound rule in dry races?

options.text: To force pit stops and mix up the race; a one-stop would be boring and predictable.
options.explanation: Right. The rule exists to prevent running the whole race on one soft tyre set. It creates strategy.

options.text: To save tyres and reduce the environmental impact.
options.explanation: The rule is not about tyre conservation. It is about race strategy and competition.

options.text: Hard and medium tyres are always faster than soft.
options.explanation: No. Softs are the fastest tyre. The rule forces variety.

options.text: To make pit crews work more and tire them out.
options.explanation: That is not the reason. The rule is about race fairness and strategy.

explanation.correct: Right. The two-compound rule exists to force stops and prevent a dull one-stop winner. It creates drama and strategy.
explanation.incorrect: The two-compound rule forces drivers to use at least two different compounds, which forces at least one stop per race.
explanation.sayThisLine: The two-compound rule forces a stop.

payload.prompt: In a wet race, does the two-compound rule still apply?

options.text: No. In wet races, drivers can stay on inters or wets all race and no stop is mandatory.
options.explanation: Right. The two-compound rule applies to dry races only. Wet races have different rules.

options.text: Yes, the two-compound rule always applies no matter the weather.
options.explanation: Wrong. Wet races don't have the same rule; the focus is on safety and tyre choice.

options.text: The driver can choose to ignore it if it is too wet.
options.explanation: No. The rule is lifted in wet races, not chosen to ignore.

options.text: Only the leading car has to follow the two-compound rule.
options.explanation: All cars follow the same rules, including the two-compound rule in dry races.

explanation.correct: Right. The two-compound rule is for dry races. In wet races, drivers can pit for different compounds as weather demands.
explanation.incorrect: The two-compound rule exists for dry races to force strategy. Wet races have different tyre-choice rules.
explanation.sayThisLine: The two-compound rule does not apply in the wet.

payload.prompt: Can a driver run a one-stop race by starting on soft and finishing on hard?

scene.alt: A two-stint race chart: soft tyres (red) for the first 30 laps, hard tyres (white) for the last 20 laps.

explanation.correct: Right. Soft, then hard is two compounds, so it satisfies the rule and is a one-stop strategy.
explanation.incorrect: Starting on soft and stopping for hard is two compounds. That is a legal one-stop under the two-compound rule.

payload.prompt: Is starting on hard and finishing on medium also two different compounds?

scene.alt: A two-stint race: hard (white) for 25 laps, then medium (yellow) for 30 laps.

explanation.correct: Right. Hard and medium are two different compounds, so the two-compound rule is met.
explanation.incorrect: Hard and medium are two different tyre compounds, so this satisfies the rule.

payload.prompt: Is a one-stop strategy faster or slower than a two-stop in the same race?

facts.label: One-stop
facts.value: Soft first (30 laps), hard second (20 laps).

options.label: One-stop is faster
options.consequence: If tyres last, one-stop saves 20 seconds of pit loss compared to two stops and finishes ahead.
considerations: One-stop avoids the second stop's time loss.
But old tyres on the last laps cost speed.

options.label: Two-stop is faster
options.consequence: Fresher tyres multiple times mean better pace throughout. The two stops cost time but the speed gain pays for it.
considerations: Two stops cost 40 seconds total pit loss.
But younger tyres mean pace gains that cover the loss.

payload.expertNote: Strategy choices depend on track, weather and tyre life. Generally, two stops win if tyre life is short; one-stop wins if the tyres last the full stint.
payload.sayThisLine: The one-stop beats the two-stop if the tyres hold out.

lessons.title: Undercut and overcut: first taste
lessons.objective: Predict who comes out ahead after a rival stops.

payload.prompt: What is an undercut in pit strategy?

options.text: Pitting first to gain time on fresh tyres and jump ahead when the rival stops.
options.explanation: Right. Undercut is pitting early to gain a place through speed on new tyres.

options.text: Staying out longer than a rival to gain track position.
options.explanation: That is the opposite; that is an overcut.

options.text: Cutting the braking into a corner.
options.explanation: That is a driving term, not a strategy term.

options.text: Using a harder tyre than a rival to last longer.
options.explanation: That is a compound choice, not an undercut.

explanation.correct: Right. An undercut is pitting first: you get fresh tyres and a quick lap, so you jump ahead when the rival stops.
explanation.incorrect: An undercut means pitting first so your fresh tyres give you a pace advantage before the rival pits.
explanation.sayThisLine: They went for the undercut and it worked.

payload.prompt: What is an overcut in strategy?

options.text: Staying out longer while a rival pits, then using clear air to be faster on old tyres.
options.explanation: Right. Overcut is pitting late to gain a gap and time on clear track.

options.text: Pitting first to jump ahead.
options.explanation: That is the undercut, not the overcut.

options.text: Using the same tyres as a rival.
options.explanation: That is not strategy, that is tyre matching.

options.text: Exceeding the speed limit in the pit lane.
options.explanation: That is a pit-lane infraction, not a strategy term.

explanation.correct: Right. An overcut is pitting late: you stay out, the rival stops, and you get a clear run to build a gap.
explanation.incorrect: An overcut is staying out longer than the rival. When they pit, you get clean air and can be faster.
explanation.sayThisLine: The overcut can work if you get clear air.

payload.prompt: You are one second behind on track. Should you undercut to try to get ahead?

facts.label: Your tyres
facts.value: In the pit window now; can run four more laps.

facts.label: Undercut gain
facts.value: Fresh tyres worth 1.5 seconds per lap for the next lap, then 0.5 seconds.

options.label: Undercut now
options.consequence: Pit now, lose 20 seconds, gain 1.5 seconds on the first quick lap and 0.5 on the next. After two laps you are still behind, but you have fresher tyres than the rival and can push.
considerations: The undercut is worth doing if you think fresh tyres buy you back the gap.

options.label: Stay out and overcut
options.consequence: Staying out loses you the gap immediately. The rival undercuts you and jumps ahead. You cannot win the overcut if you give up the lead.
considerations: Trailing by one second, the undercut is your chance.

payload.expertNote: Undercut works best when you are close enough that the gap can be overcome by fresh tyre pace advantage.

lessons.title: Reading a pit wall call
lessons.objective: Decode a pit call and the trade-offs behind it.

payload.prompt: Your race engineer says: 'Box box, this lap, soft tyres, we are in the pit window.' Explain it back in plain English.

suggestions.text: Got it: I am coming in this lap for fresh soft tyres because now is the right time to stop.
suggestions.explanation: Perfect. You restated it clearly: pit this lap, fresh softs, and it is strategic timing.
Right action, but you skipped the 'why': the pit window is the strategy timing that matters.
Box box is the radio call to pit this lap. It means come in now.

explanation.correct: Right. Box box means come in this lap, and the pit window is the team's signal that now is the right strategic moment.
explanation.incorrect: Box box is the call to pit this lap. The pit window is the range of laps where a stop makes sense strategically.
explanation.sayThisLine: Box box, this lap, pit now.

payload.prompt: The engineer also says: 'We are closing the pit window. One more lap and it shuts.' What does that mean for you?

suggestions.text: The pit window is closing soon. If I don't pit next lap, I will miss it and fall behind rival plans.
suggestions.explanation: Excellent. You understood that missing the window means losing the strategic advantage.
Right, but you didn't say why it matters: missing the window loses the strategy.
The pit window is the range of laps where a stop makes strategic sense. Too early is wasting tyres; too late is losing the undercut.

explanation.correct: Right. The pit window is a timing window. Miss it and your stop is no longer strategically sound.
explanation.incorrect: A pit window is the optimal range of laps to stop. Pit outside it and you lose the advantage (early) or the gap (late).
explanation.sayThisLine: One more lap or we close the pit window.

payload.prompt: The pit wall calls box box, but the safety car is about to deploy. What happens to the pit window?

options.text: The pit window widens because the field will bunch and everyone will pit. Stacking happens.
options.explanation: Right. A safety car creates a scramble for pit slots. The window opens up to fit more cars.

options.text: The pit window closes because no one can pit under the safety car.
options.explanation: Wrong. Pitting under the safety car is allowed and often happens.

options.text: The pit window stays the same as before.
options.explanation: No. A safety car changes everything. The bunching changes the strategic timing.

options.text: The pit window moves later in the race.
options.explanation: Depends on the safety car timing, but generally the window opens immediately when the car deploys.

explanation.correct: Right. A safety car bunches the field and all teams want to pit. The pit window expands and pit stops are now 'free' relative to the time gained.
explanation.incorrect: A safety car changes the pit window because the field bunches. Suddenly, pitting under the safety car is strategic gold.
explanation.sayThisLine: Safety car is out, the pit window blew open.

payload.prompt: You are leading by five seconds when the pit wall calls box box. You pit, lose 20 seconds, but gain 1.5 seconds on fresh soft tyres. Where are you now?

options.text: Behind by about 13 seconds (5 - 20 + 1.5 = -13.5).
options.explanation: Right. You lose the lead, fall behind, but the call was correct if it sets up for a later win.

options.text: Still leading by five seconds because the pit crew was fast.
options.explanation: No. The math is clear: pit loss is 20 seconds, gain is 1.5. You lose the lead.

options.text: Behind by 20 seconds because that is the pit loss.
options.explanation: Close, but don't forget the 1.5 seconds you gain back on the quick lap with fresh softs.

options.text: The position depends on whether the rival pits at the same time.
options.explanation: True in general, but for this math, the answer is clear: about 13 seconds down.

explanation.correct: Right. You lose the lead in the stop, but the team calls it because the plan is to regain it later with fresher tyres.
explanation.incorrect: Pit loss is 20 seconds, so you fall behind when you stop. But fresh tyres gain the time back eventually.
explanation.sayThisLine: The stop cost the lead but we got fresh tyres.
